bib.title: Beyond the Leaderboard: A Synthesis of Tool-Use, Planning, and Reasoning Failures in Large Language Model Agents

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Beyond the Leaderboard: A Synthesis of Tool-Use, Planning, and Reasoning Failures in Large Language Model Agents". Wael Albayaydh, Rui Zhao, Ivan Flechais (all University of Oxford). arXiv 2607.05775, preprint. The text prints no date. The arXiv ID implies July 2026, and the latest reference is 2026. The paper calls itself "a narrative synthesis, not a formal systematic review".

COVERAGE: 61,709 of 61,709 chars read, all 16 pages, including Table 2, limitations and the reference list. Nothing was skipped. One extraction caveat: Figure 1 is an image, so only its caption was extracted.

TARGET NOTE (06-evaluating-agents.md, 12.4k words, `confidence: high`, `cleaned: 2026-11-01`)
- Best-fit section: "Evaluate the components, then the whole", with a secondary hook in "Non-determinism" and "Efficiency metrics". The paper is a secondary survey of failure modes. It is not a method for grading agents.
- The note already covers these points, each with its own primary source:
  - HAL (arXiv:2510.11977, line 376): 21,730 rollouts, 9 models, 9 benchmarks, about $40k, and 21 of 36 same-scaffold comparisons where a higher reasoning setting gave equal or lower accuracy.
  - Outcome vs trajectory, partial credit, component ceilings, pass^k, cost per success.
  - Contamination, in 12-failure-modes.md.
- The note lacks these points:
  - No SWE-bench leakage or weak-test-suite correction.
  - No METR time-horizon claim.
  - No TravelPlanner joint-constraint result.
  - No MAST multi-agent failure taxonomy, and no ToolEmu or InjecAgent safety rates.
  - No tool-error taxonomy (ToolScan).
  - No sub-skill non-composability as a general principle.
- Better-fit notes:
  - 12-failure-modes.md fits the SWE-bench leakage and test-suite audit (it has a "Contamination" section).
  - 09-reading-results.md fits the "headline score includes measurement error" theme.
  - The ToolEmu and InjecAgent numbers belong in the adversarial or safety area. 06 only touches the adversarial suite in one line.
- Recommendation: cite the paper as "sharpens" in 06 and in 12-failure-modes.md, per the repo rule. Follow secondary figures to their primaries (Aleithan, Yu, Kwa, Cemri) before using any number in a note.

CORE CLAIM: Across 27 benchmark, taxonomy and audit papers (2023-2026, 19 benchmarks), agent failures fall into six clusters: tool invocation, planning and constraints, long-horizon degradation, multi-agent coordination, safety, and measurement validity. Failure compounds non-linearly with task length, sub-skill competence does not compose into end-to-end success, and scaffolding does not uniformly help. Some of the apparent leaderboard progress is correction of measurement error.

CLAIMS (ranked). Everything here is a figure reported by others and not re-run by the authors (§6, §9). Setups are therefore the cited studies' setups, and the paper gives few details: no n, runs or grader for most of them.
1. SWE-bench corrections
   - Leakage and weak tests: a representative SWE-agent configuration's success rate fell from about 12.5% to about 4% after correction (Aleithan 2024, SWE-Bench+). Quote: "the reported success rate of a representative SWE -agent configuration fall from approximately 12.5% to approximately 4% (Aleithan et al., 2024)". Where: §4.6.
   - Test augmentation: stronger generated tests changed leaderboard rankings in about 25-41% of cases across SWE-bench Lite and Verified (Yu 2025, UTBoost). Quote: "changed leaderboard rankings in approximately 25-41% of cases across SWE-bench Lite and Verified". Where: §4.6.
   - Both figures are for one configuration or one pair of subsets. Neither model nor n is given.
2. TravelPlanner (Xie 2024) final-plan success. Quote: "GPT-4 achieved only a 0.6% final-plan success rate on multi-day travel itineraries". Where: §4.2.
   - Table 2 reads "0.6% (GPT-4); ~10% (o1-preview); ~65% (best verifier-augmented configuration)".
   - The 65% comes from arXiv:2404.11891 and uses a formal-verifier configuration, with no n given.
   - The text says per-constraint satisfaction is "far higher", with no number.
3. METR time horizon (Kwa 2025). Quote: "near -100% success on tasks that take skilled humans under approximately four minutes, but succeed less than 10% of the time on tasks taking humans more than approximately four hours". The 50% horizon "doubling roughly every seven months since 2019". Where: §4.3. The paper adds that METR attributes the gains mainly to reliability and error recovery.
4. Long-context web agents (arXiv:2512.04307). Quote: "success rates reaching 40-50% on short-horizon variants of a task can fall to below 10% once the same task is embedded in a longer interaction history". Where: §4.3. LoCoBench-Agent (arXiv:2511.13998) reports "~3-5% loss per 50% length increase" (Table 2 only). The two sources are not quite consistent in kind.
5. MAST (Cemri 2025). Seven frameworks, over 200 tasks, manual trace annotation with Cohen's Kappa 0.88, fourteen failure modes in three categories. Quote: "approximately 42% and 37% respectively in one reported breakdown". Table 2 gives about 21% for verification and termination. Where: §4.4. Multi-agent gains over single-agent were "frequently minimal".
6. Safety
   - ToolEmu (Ruan 2023): 36 toolkits, 144 test cases, LM-emulated sandbox. Quote: "Even the safest evaluated agent in that study exhibited failures with potentially severe outcomes in 23.9% of test cases". The evaluator's findings were confirmed valid by humans for "68.8%". Where: §4.5.
   - InjecAgent (Zhan 2024): 1,054 test cases. Quote: "a standard ReAct-prompted GPT-4 agent was vulnerable approximately 24% of the time, rising to approximately 47% with a reinforced attack prompt". Open models without safety tuning exceed 80% in some configurations. Where: §4.5.
7. Test-time scaling (General AgentBench, arXiv:2602.18998). Ten agents. Quote: "neither scaling approach reliably improved performance". Explanations offered: a "context ceiling" and a "verification gap". Where: §4.2.
8. HAL (Kapoor 2025). Quote: "over 21,000 agent rollouts across nine models and nine benchmarks at a cost of approximately $40,000", with "higher reasoning effort reduced accuracy in the majority of runs". Where: §4.6. This duplicates the note, which has the sharper 21 of 36.
9. Tool-use errors
   - ToolScan has seven error types.
   - Quote: "approximately 77.5 versus 21 incorrect calls on average". Where: §4.1.
   - This is the BFCL multiple-function-call category, with native function-calling mode producing more incorrect calls than prompting. The paper gives no model names or n.
   - NoisyToolBench: models fabricate missing parameters rather than asking.
10. Genuine progress (§5)
   - WebArena: about 14% to 61.7% against human performance of about 78% (Marreed 2025, one enterprise scaffold).
   - WebVoyager: "approximately 85-90%" on filtered subsets.
   - SWE-bench raw leaderboards: about 20% (2024) to "50-60%+" (2026).
   - Safety fine-tuning lowers injection vulnerability.

LIMITS
- Stated (§9):
  - It is a narrative review and not pre-registered.
  - Cluster boundaries are subjective.
  - Figures may be superseded.
  - No experiments were reproduced.
  - English, text and web tasks only.
  - A few non-peer-reviewed sources are used.
- Unstated:
  - No grader, run count or model list for most figures. Models are named only for GPT-4 (TravelPlanner, InjecAgent) and o1-preview.
  - The convergence argument for the taxonomy's validity (§3.3) is the authors' own and is not tested.
  - Several references are bare or incomplete: unnamed "Towards a science of AI agent reliability", no authors on the final entries, no arXiv ID for the Aleithan reference.
  - Frontier results are mostly 2024-25 and may have dated.
  - The smart-home bystander-privacy digression (§4.5) is the authors' own prior work and is not evidence about agents.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES
- WebVoyager is given as "85-90%" in §5.2 but "57-90%" in Table 2.
- "Majority of runs" for HAL reasoning effort is loose. The note has 21 of 36.
- The abstract says 27 papers, but the Table 1 category counts sum to 31, which they explain as overlap.
- "Reasoning models" are credited for TravelPlanner gains, but the 65% figure comes from a formal-verifier setup, so scaffolding is doing the work.
- The paper says scaffolding does not uniformly help, yet its headline TravelPlanner gain from 0.6% to 65% is scaffolding-driven. §7.4 half-acknowledges this.
- It describes METR as "peer-reviewed-adjacent" but cites it as a preprint.
- Table 2 attributes the SWE-bench correction to three papers, but only the 12.5% to 4% figure has a named source.

BUILDS ON: Toolformer (Schick 2023), ReAct (Yao 2023), Reflexion (Shinn 2023), AgentBench (Liu 2023), TravelPlanner (Xie 2024), BFCL (Patil 2025), ToolScan (Kokane 2024), MAST (Cemri 2025), METR (Kwa 2025), HAL (Kapoor 2025), ToolEmu (Ruan 2023), InjecAgent (Zhan 2024), SWE-Bench+ (Aleithan 2024), UTBoost (Yu 2025), compositionality gap (Press 2023), Wooldridge (2009).

CODE: none.

FIGURES: Figure 1 (p5), "The six failure clusters mapped onto distinct stages of an LLM agent's reasoning-to-action pipeline, as derived in Section 3.3." It is a schematic that would work as a diagnostic map from symptom to pipeline stage (tool parameters, plan, state, inter-agent, safety, measurement). I read only the caption. Table 2 (p10-11) is the other candidate, but as a table rather than a figure.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- Text extraction is clean apart from hyphen-spacing artifacts.
- The paper's date is not printed.
- Four statements could not be verified from the text: the model behind the 77.5 vs 21 figure, n for the 65% TravelPlanner figure, the grader and n for the web-agent percentages, and the scale of the 12.5% to 4% correction.
- A temporary extract of the table section sits in /tmp/alb/rest.txt.
